title: A crayfish contest leads to a science puzzle
summary:
Biologist Caitlin Bloomer found a huge crayfish in the mud in Kentucky. Its kind is called the Crawzilla crawdad. She was sure it was the biggest crayfish ever.

But a coworker said, "No way, I've caught bigger." So Bloomer started a search across the country. She asked museums and scientists to check their collections for giant crayfish. The team used special tools called calipers to measure them carefully. They found 20 extra-large crayfish from 18 kinds.

Bloomer's Crawzilla made the top 20. The winner was a Tennessee bottlebrush crayfish kept at West Liberty University in West Virginia. Its body was 86.6 millimeters long, about 3.4 inches, not counting its tail and claws.

The scientists also found a puzzle. The biggest crayfish of many kinds stopped growing at about 80 millimeters. Their hard outer shells or their muscles might keep them from growing bigger.
why_it_matters: Even a friendly contest can lead to real science, showing that being curious about animals you find outside can teach us something new.

keywords.explanation: A biologist is a scientist who studies living things.
Museums are places that collect and show important objects, including animals kept for study.
Calipers are tools that measure the size of something very carefully.
Millimeters are very small units used to measure length.
Muscles are body parts that help animals move.

background_read: Crayfish, also called crawdads, are small freshwater animals related to lobsters.
A crayfish has a hard outer shell, and it must shed that shell to grow bigger.
Museums keep animals for many years so scientists can measure and compare them later.
